title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells
ru: Изобретатель путешествует в далёкое будущее и встречает элоев и морлоков

chapters.title: Chapter 1. The Machine on the Table
chapters.text:
The Time Traveller (I will call him that, because I never found a better name for him) was explaining something strange to us. His grey eyes were shining, and his face, usually pale, was pink with excitement. The fire was burning brightly, and the lamps made little silver lights in our glasses. It was after dinner at his house in Richmond, and we were all in a lazy, comfortable mood.

There were five of us that evening: a doctor, a psychologist, a mayor from a small country town, a young man called Filby, who loved to argue, and myself.

“Listen carefully,” the Time Traveller said, holding up one thin finger. “Everything around us has length, width and height. This box, for example. But can a box exist for no time at all? Of course not. So everything has a fourth direction too. And that direction is Time.”

“Of course,” said the doctor politely, looking at his cigar.

“But we can't move about in Time,” said the psychologist. “I can walk to the left or to the right. I can climb a ladder. But I can't walk into tomorrow, or back into yesterday.”

“Can't you?” said the Time Traveller. “When you remember something very clearly, you jump back to it for a moment. A hundred years ago, men couldn't go up into the sky. Now we have balloons. Why should Time be different?”

Filby laughed. “Because it's nonsense, that's why.”

“Is it?” The Time Traveller smiled. “I have been working on this question for years. And I have built a machine.”

Nobody said anything. Then the mayor asked, “To travel in Time?”

“Wait here.”

He left the room. We heard his slippers in the long passage that led to his workshop.

When he came back, he was carrying a small, shining object, about the size of a clock. He put it on a little table by the fire. It was a beautiful thing, made of metal, ivory and something clear, like crystal. There was a tiny seat in it, and two small levers — the kind of handles that you push or pull to make a machine work.

“This is only a model,” he said. “It took me two years to make. When I push this lever forward, the machine will travel into the future. This other lever sends it into the past. Now look closely, all of you. I don't want anyone to say afterwards that it was a trick.”

He took the psychologist's hand and put his finger on the little lever. “You do it.”

The psychologist pushed. There was a breath of wind, and the lamp flame jumped. The little machine turned round, became a shadow, a faint ghost of brass and ivory — and it was gone. The table was empty.

For a moment nobody spoke. Then the doctor got down on his knees and looked under the table. The Time Traveller only laughed and lit his pipe.

“It's gone into the future,” he said.

“But if it's travelling into the future,” said the psychologist slowly, “it should still be here. Why can't we see it?”

“Because it's moving through Time so fast. Can you see a bullet flying through the air? No. It's there, but it's too fast for your eyes. My machine is the same.”

Then he stood up. “Would you like to see the real one?”

He took a lamp and led us down the passage to his workshop. There, in the yellow light, stood a much larger copy of the little machine. It had a saddle, big enough for a man, and a few parts were still lying on the bench, unfinished.

“Look here,” said the doctor. “Are you serious? Or is this a trick, like that ghost you showed us last Christmas?”

The Time Traveller held the lamp high. “Upon that machine,” he said, “I intend to explore Time. I was never more serious in my life.”

None of us believed him, of course. He was a clever man, but he loved tricks and jokes. We walked home that night laughing.

The next Thursday, we found out how wrong we were.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Traveller Comes Home
chapters.text:
A week later, I went to Richmond again. The doctor and the psychologist were there, with two new guests: a newspaper editor and a journalist. But our host was missing. His servant gave us a note. “If I'm late,” it said, “start dinner at seven. I'll explain when I come.”

We started without him. The editor was telling a funny story when the door opened slowly.

The Time Traveller stood there, and I almost didn't know him. His coat was dirty and torn, and his hair was grey with dust. There was a cut on his chin, and his face was white, like the face of a man who has suffered terribly. He was limping, and on his feet he wore only torn, bloody socks.

“Good heavens, man!” said the doctor. “What's happened to you?”

The Time Traveller smiled weakly. “Don't worry. I'm all right.” He held out his hand for a glass of wine and drank it in one go. “That's better. I'm starving. I'd like some meat.”

He went upstairs to wash and change. When he came back, he ate like a hungry dog, and none of us dared to ask a question. At last he pushed his plate away.

“I'll tell you everything,” he said. “But you mustn't interrupt me. It will sound like lies, but it's true. Since this morning, I've lived eight days — days that no other man has ever lived.”

This is his story, as he told it to us that night. I will use his own words.

At ten o'clock this morning, the machine was ready. I sat in the saddle and pushed the starting lever a little.

For a moment I felt sick, as if I was falling in a dream. I looked round. Had nothing happened? Then I looked at the clock. A moment ago it had said ten past ten. Now it said half past three!

I pushed the lever harder. The room went dark. My housekeeper, Mrs Watchett, came in and shot across the room like a rocket. Night came like someone turning off a lamp. Then morning. Then night again, faster and faster. Soon the sun was jumping across the sky, once every minute, and every minute was a day.

It was like riding a wild horse at full speed. The walls of my workshop disappeared, and I was in the open air. I watched trees grow up like puffs of smoke and die. Huge buildings rose round me, beautiful and strange, and then melted away like dreams. The dials on my machine, which counted the days in thousands and millions, were spinning wildly.

Then a terrible thought came to me. What would happen when I stopped? If there was a wall or a tree in the same place, my body would crash into it, atom into atom. There would be a huge explosion, and I would be blown into nothingness.

I panicked. I pulled the lever back too hard. The machine turned over, and I was thrown through the air.

I was sitting on soft grass. Hailstones as big as cherries were falling round me, hissing on the leaves. “A fine welcome,” I said, “to a man who has travelled thousands of years to see you!”

I looked at the dials. The year was 802,701. I had travelled eight hundred thousand years into the future!

Through the grey curtain of hail, I saw something huge. It was a great white statue, standing on a bronze base. It was a sphinx — the creature from old Egyptian stories, with a lion's body and a human head — but this one had wide wings. Its face was turned towards me, and it seemed to smile — a cold, unpleasant smile.

Then I was afraid. What had happened to the human race? What if men had become cruel, and much stronger than me? To them, I might look like a wild animal — something to kill.

I began to turn the machine the right way up again. The hail stopped, and the sun came out. Then I saw them. Figures in soft, bright clothes were coming out of a great building on the hill.

One of them was walking straight towards me.

chapters.title: Chapter 3. The Children of the Future
chapters.text:
He was a small creature, only about four feet tall, in a purple tunic. He was beautiful and delicate, like a little china doll. His skin was pink and smooth, his hair was curly, and his eyes were large and gentle.

Suddenly I wasn't afraid any more. A man like that could never hurt me. I felt I could throw a dozen of them across the garden.

Soon there were eight or ten of these little people round me. They laughed and talked to each other in a soft, sweet language, like birdsong. They touched my hands and face with their soft fingers, as if they wanted to be sure that I was real.

Then some of them began to touch the Time Machine, and that frightened me. Quickly, I unscrewed the two little levers and put them in my pocket. Without the levers, nobody could start the machine.

One of them pointed at the sun and then made a sound like thunder. He was asking me if I had come down from the sun in the storm! I felt a sudden, cold disappointment. These beautiful people had the minds of five-year-old children.

They led me, laughing, into a huge grey building. Inside was a long hall with coloured windows. The floor was worn into deep paths by thousands of years of feet. There were no chairs, only soft cushions and long stone tables covered with fruit. My hosts sat down to eat, throwing the skins and seeds on the floor, and invited me to join them.

I was hungry, so I did. Later I learned that they ate nothing but fruit. There were no horses, no cows, no sheep — all the animals had gone.

After dinner, I tried to learn their language. I pointed at a piece of fruit and asked its name. They thought this was the funniest game in the world. But after ten minutes they got tired, like small children, and wandered away. Later I found out that they called themselves the Eloi.

Then I walked alone up a hill to look at this new world. The sun was going down. Everywhere I saw palaces and ruins among the trees, but no small houses and no shops. The whole Earth had become one huge garden. There were no weeds and no biting insects, and I saw nobody who was old or ill.

There I made my first theory. Humanity, I thought, had won its battle with nature. There was no more danger, no more hard work. But danger is what makes us strong and clever. Without it, people had grown weak, gentle and stupid. It was the sunset of mankind.

I was wrong, of course. But I didn't know that yet.

As it was getting dark, I came down the hill towards the white sphinx, looking for my machine on the lawn.

The lawn was empty. The Time Machine was gone.

I felt as if someone had hit me in the stomach. I ran round the lawn like a madman. Without the machine, I could never go home. I would be trapped here for ever.

I ran into the great hall, where the Eloi were sleeping in the dark. I struck a match and shouted, “Where is my machine?” They woke up and looked at me with terror. Some of them ran away. I grabbed one and shook him. Then I felt ashamed. They didn't understand a word.

At last, tired and hopeless, I fell asleep on the grass.

In the morning, calmer now, I looked carefully at the lawn. There were long marks in the grass, as if something heavy had been pulled across it. The marks went straight to the bronze base of the sphinx — and stopped. In the base were two bronze doors, firmly shut. I pushed and hit them, but they wouldn't move.

My machine was inside. Someone had dragged it there.

But who? The Eloi were far too weak to move it. When I pointed at the doors and asked them, they looked away with strange, frightened faces.

There was someone else in this world. Someone the Eloi were afraid of.

chapters.title: Chapter 4. Weena and the Wells
chapters.text:
A few days later, I was watching some of the Eloi swimming in the river. Suddenly one of them, a small girl, got a cramp in her leg, and the river began to carry her away. She was crying for help. The others just watched.

I jumped into the river, caught her, and pulled her out onto the bank. Soon she was all right.

Her name was Weena. From that moment, she followed me everywhere, like a little dog. She brought me flowers and put them in my pockets. She cried whenever I left her behind. I can't tell you how much it meant to me. In that strange, lonely world, she was my only friend.

Through Weena, I learned something important: the Eloi were afraid of the dark. At night they never went outside, and they never slept alone, only in large groups in the great halls.

All over the country there were round wells — deep holes with a little roof over them. When I looked down into one, I couldn't see any water. But I could hear a deep sound — thud, thud, thud — like a huge engine, far below. And air was moving down into the hole, as if something was breathing.

One morning before sunrise, I saw some white shapes on the hill, like small apes. They were carrying something dark between them. I was half asleep, and I told myself it was a dream.

But it wasn't. A few days later, I was resting from the heat in a ruined building when I saw two eyes in the shadows — big, red, shining eyes. A small white creature, like a strange ape, ran past me. It had pale skin, the colour of a worm, and long hair on its head and back. It ran to a well and disappeared down a ladder of iron hooks in the wall.

Now I began to understand. Over hundreds of thousands of years, humanity had split into two species. Above the ground lived the Eloi, pretty and useless. Below the ground lived these pale creatures of the dark. The Eloi called them Morlocks. These creatures worked the machines, and the thudding noise in the wells came from their factories.

I thought of my own time. Even in London today, many workers spend their days underground, building railways and running machines, while the rich enjoy the sunlight. Had this simply gone on for eight hundred thousand years? Had the workers forgotten the sun completely?

And where was my Time Machine? The Morlocks must have taken it. So I had to go down.

Weena pulled at my hands and cried, but I gently pushed her away and climbed into the well.

The hooks were thin and rusty, and the hole went down and down. My arms began to ache. One hook bent under my weight, and I almost fell into the darkness. Above me, the circle of blue sky became smaller and smaller.

At last, I reached a tunnel in the wall. It was hot, and the air smelled of oil and something else — something like fresh blood. I struck a match. Pale faces with huge eyes turned towards me, and the Morlocks ran back from the light. I had only two matches left — no lamp, no gun, nothing else. How stupid I had been!

In the light of the second match, I saw a great cave full of machines. In the middle stood a table with a large piece of red meat on it.

Then the match went out. In the darkness, I felt soft, cold hands touching me. They pulled at my coat and my pockets. I struck my third match, and they ran. I ran back to the tunnel and began to climb.

A Morlock caught my foot and held on. I kicked hard, again and again, until he fell away. At last I pulled myself out into the sunlight, shaking and sick.

Weena was there, waiting for me. She was crying with joy.

But I couldn't stop thinking about that table. In this world, there were no cows, no pigs, no sheep.

So where did the Morlocks get their meat?

chapters.title: Chapter 5. Fire in the Forest
chapters.text:
Slowly, the terrible truth came to me. The Morlocks made the Eloi's clothes. They kept them safe and well fed, as a farmer keeps his cattle. And on dark nights, when there was no moon, they came up from their wells and took them away. The Eloi were their food.

I remembered the white shapes on the hill, carrying something dark between them. I felt sick. And every night, the moon was getting thinner. The dark nights were coming.

I needed a weapon, and I needed a safe place to sleep. Some days before, I had seen a huge green building far away. So I set off for it with Weena on my shoulders.

It was a ruined palace of green stone — once, I soon understood, a museum. There were giant dinosaur bones, rusty machines, and a library where all the books had turned to brown dust. All those dreams, all that work — and nothing was left.

But I found treasures there. In a sealed glass case was a box of matches, still dry after thousands of years. I also found a piece of camphor — a kind of white wax that burns very well — and I pulled a heavy iron bar from an old machine. Now I had a weapon.

In the darker galleries I heard soft footsteps. The Morlocks were near. We left in the late afternoon, and I decided to take a short cut back through a forest. It was a terrible mistake.

Night fell while we were still among the trees — the first night without a moon. Soon I heard them all round us: soft feet, quiet voices, the touch of cold fingers on my arm.

I made a fire with dry sticks and some of the camphor. The Morlocks ran back from the light, and I saw their eyes shining red between the trees. Weena had never seen a big fire before. She wanted to run and play with the red flames, and I had to hold her back.

We moved on, and later I made a second fire. Then I sat down to rest — and, to my horror, I fell asleep.

When I opened my eyes, everything was black. The fire had gone out. Hands were holding me everywhere, and teeth bit my neck. My box of matches was gone. And Weena was gone.

I jumped up, swinging the iron bar. I felt it hit soft bodies and heard bones break. For a moment, I was free.

Then I saw a red light between the trees. My first fire had spread into the dry forest! The flames came closer every second, and in their terrible light I saw that the Morlocks were helpless. The light blinded them. They ran into trees, into each other, even into the fire. At first I hit them, but soon I felt only pity.

I called Weena's name again and again, but I never found her. Perhaps the Morlocks had taken her. Perhaps she had died in the fire. I will never know.

In the morning, alone and almost broken, I walked back to the white sphinx. I had nothing left but my iron bar and a few matches from the museum box, loose in my pocket.

The bronze doors of the sphinx were open. Inside, in a small dark room, stood my Time Machine.

It was a trap, of course. But I didn't care. I stepped inside, and at once the doors closed behind me with a loud clang. I was in total darkness.

I heard the Morlocks laughing softly as they came closer. I tried to strike a match on the wall. Nothing. The museum matches were the kind that light only on their own box.

Hands grabbed my arms and legs. Fighting them off, I found the levers in my pocket and pushed them into place.

I threw myself into the saddle and pulled the lever.

The hands fell away. The darkness turned to grey light. I was free!

Then I looked at the dials, and my heart went cold. In the fight, I had moved the lever the wrong way. I was not going home. I was rushing deeper and deeper into the future.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. The Last Beach
chapters.text:
I could have stopped and turned back. But a strange, cold curiosity held me. How would the world end? I let the machine run on.

The years flashed past, then thousands of years, then millions. Slowly, the days grew longer. At last the sun stopped moving. It hung low over the sea, huge and red, and didn't move at all. The Earth had almost stopped turning.

I pulled the lever back gently and stopped.

I was on a beach. The sky was dark red, with a few stars in it. The sea was still and heavy, like oil, without a single wave. The rocks were covered with green slime — the only plant life I could see. The air was so thin that it was hard to breathe.

A huge white thing, like a giant butterfly, flew screaming into the sky.

Something touched my neck. I turned — and saw a monster. It was a crab as big as a table, with long feelers waving in the air. Its eyes moved on thin stalks, and its mouth was working hungrily. Behind it, more of them were crawling slowly across the beach.

I pushed the lever and escaped, travelling on a thousand years at a time. Each time I stopped, the sun was bigger and darker, and the world was colder.

At last, more than thirty million years in the future, I stopped once more. The crabs had gone. Snow was falling, and the only sound was the cold wind.

Then the sun began to disappear. Something was moving across it — perhaps the moon, perhaps a planet. The world grew darker and darker, until there was only a thin red line of light. The silence was terrible. All the sounds of life — birds, sheep, the voices of children — had gone for ever.

As the light came back, I saw something move on the shore. It was a round black thing, about the size of a football, with long arms hanging from it. It was hopping about in the red water.

I felt sick with fear, and with something worse — a terrible loneliness. This was the end of everything. With shaking hands, I turned the machine back towards home.

The journey back seemed endless. At last I saw the walls of my workshop round me again. I saw Mrs Watchett walk backwards across the room. I stopped the machine, and here I am.

That was the end of his story.

Nobody said anything for a long time. Then the editor laughed. “What a pity you're not a writer of stories!” he said.

“You don't believe me,” said the Time Traveller quietly. “Sometimes I don't believe it myself.” He took two strange white flowers out of his pocket and placed them on the table. “Weena put these in my pocket.”

The doctor looked at them closely. “I've never seen flowers like these,” he said slowly.

The others went home, laughing a little, as people do when they are uncomfortable. But I couldn't stop thinking about the story. The next day I went back to Richmond.

The Time Traveller met me in the hall, with a small camera under his arm. “Wait for me,” he said. “I'll be back in half an hour — with proof. Photographs!”

He went into the workshop. A minute later, I heard a strange sound and the noise of breaking glass. I opened the door. For a second I saw a ghostly shape — and then nothing. The Time Machine was gone.

I waited for him, as he had asked. That was three years ago. He has never come back.

Where is he now? Perhaps he is among the Eloi again. Perhaps he has gone back to the age of the dinosaurs. Perhaps he is lying on some dark, cold beach at the end of the world. I will never know.

But I still have the two white flowers. He left them on the table that night. They are brown and dry now. They remind me that even when the mind and strength of humanity had gone, gratitude and love still lived on in the human heart.
